column3: Directly pairs success with self-purification, specifying a core quality of believers.
Connects faithfulness and good conduct to a great reward, but only indirectly to success.
Contrasts crisis-driven profession of faith with the settled belief named in the focus.
Directly states success for the one who purifies the self, reinforcing 87:14.
Within the same surah, exposes denial of God's lordship rather than defining believers' success.
Names piety, obedience, generosity, and freedom from greed as the way to success.
Uses claimed triumph by superiority as a contrary, provisional measure of success.
Links thankful worship to wholesome provision, a peripheral practical setting for belief.
Calls believers to piety, seeking means to God, and striving so that they may succeed.
Shows believers tested severely, adding endurance as the context in which belief is proved.
Discusses the Prophet's lack of worldly demand, without a material link to 23:1.
States that disbelievers do not succeed, providing the direct negative boundary within the surah.
Locates believers' reliance exclusively in God, a defining disposition behind their success.
Offers disciplined, non-excessive conduct, but does not closely develop success or belief.
Provides the contrary case: refusal of belief leaves many under a settled judgment.
Calls them true believers and promises rank, forgiveness, and generous provision.
False claims about God are said not to succeed, a moral boundary for the focus.
Prohibits betrayal of God, the Messenger, and trusts, identifying conduct incompatible with belief.
Makes believers a brotherhood charged with reconciliation and piety.
Directly identifies the successful as those whose scales are heavy, extending the surah's opening outcome.
Directly defines the successful through heavy scales on the Day of Judgment.
Commends Abraham's verification of the vision and good-doing, but not success explicitly.
Shows gratitude's opposite and loss of prosperity, a distant contrast to fruitful belief.
Names signs for believers but adds little beyond the focus's identity term.
Records Moses receiving his request, without a useful connection to believers' success.
Depicts final helplessness and punishment for wrongdoers, only a broad contrast.
Questions what message deniers will believe, reinforcing the negative boundary of disbelief.
Closes ethical discipline with collective repentance of believers so they may succeed.
Sets dietary prohibitions and an exception, without a distinctive link to the focus.
States that fabricators and deniers of signs do not succeed.
Commands persevering, steadfast, vigilant piety to believers so they may succeed.
Associates lawful adornment and provision with believers, but not their success.
Says criminals who fabricate or deny God's signs do not succeed.
Establishes truth in Joseph's episode, without a meaningful link to 23:1.
Concerns God's independence from human provision, not believers' success.
Marks the pain of others' unbelief, but does not illuminate the successful believers.
Protects the dignity of believers in Noah's community, a limited communal parallel.
Links grateful use of provision with a good land and forgiving Lord, indirectly fruitful conduct.
Rejects the poetic-charge and notes scant belief, a remote contrast.
Calls Abraham one of God's believing servants, but contributes little beyond the label.
Relates Abraham's fear and glad tidings, without an interpretive link.
Shows persecution directed at believers, a contextual contrast rather than success.
Calls Elijah a believing servant, redundant with the preceding identity example.
An oath by the sun that adds no useful connection on its own.
Shows faith receiving increased guidance, presenting belief as a growing divine-human response.
Limits grief over unbelief, only indirectly framing the value of belief.
Directly joins guidance from the Lord to being among the successful.
Models non-coercive separation when belief is refused, a limited boundary case.
Attributes ruin to lack of belief, repeating the negative contrast.
Questions why people do not believe, but adds little beyond other denial cards.
Displays faith through generosity and preference for others, then names such people successful.
Shows believers rejoicing in fulfillment of God's promise, a narrower outcome of faith.
Portrays God as feeding and securing a people, only tangential to believing success.
A direct address to the enwrapped Prophet without a relevant link.
Shows divergent responses to revelation and the consequence of obstruction.
States the Romans' defeat without an immediate link to the focus.
Rejects complacency before God's punishment, a secondary aspect of faithful conduct.
A direct address to the cloaked Prophet without a relevant link.
Links faith and righteous action to freedom from fear and grief, a related promise.
Defines believers' communal integrity through charitable judgment and refusal of false accusation.
Contrasts impure abundance with the good and calls for piety so that people may succeed.
Directly joins guidance from the Lord to being among the successful, though redundant with 31:5.
Defines believers by hearing and obeying divine judgment, then calls them successful.
States that magicians do not succeed, a contrast with success grounded in truth.
Calls believers to worship and do good so that they may succeed.
Models believers' reliance on God amid affliction, a supporting disposition.
Denies success to wrongdoers while tying the final outcome to divinely given guidance.
Treats fabricated-message claims as the result of unbelief, a limited negative parallel.
Identifies belief in God as the sole alleged offense of the persecuted.
Shows believers relying on God when facing possible failure.
Directly says fabricators against God do not succeed, but repeats earlier boundary cards.
Regulates believers' loyalties, a peripheral ethical implication of their identity.
Makes personal belief a public confession, but does not connect it to success.
States that wrongdoers do not succeed and defers the final outcome to judgment.
Pairs faith with righteous deeds and a superlative moral rank, broadly reinforcing the focus.
Joseph's refusal grounds moral protection in God and says wrongdoers do not succeed.
Commands avoidance of corrupting practices so that believers may succeed.
Defines true believers by unshaken faith and striving with wealth and selves.
Calls striving believers the successful and associates them with good things.
Makes divine help and reliance the believers' basis for confidence.
Forbids ridicule and stigmatizing labels after faith, clarifying believers' social ethics.
Describes a believing community's public moral role, but not the focus's success directly.
Calls existing believers to renewed faith, piety, light, and forgiveness.
Directs believers to rely on God against harmful whispering.
Distinguishes verbal profession from actual belief, sharpening the focus's identity claim.
Supplies affective, responsive, and reliant marks of true believers.
Identifies faithful care for trusts and covenants as a believerly quality.
Shows believers organized for learning and warning, a remote communal function.
Joins belief and spending, but only as a rhetorical possibility.
Calls emigrating, striving, sheltering, and aiding people true believers with forgiveness and provision.
Shows an explicit, informed confession of faith by Pharaoh's magicians.
Links repeated covenant-breaking with lack of belief, a general contrary example.
Treats later turning away as evidence that a profession of faith was unreal.
Shows Lot's faith issuing in migration toward God, a particular narrative instance.
Concerns the delivery and accounting of messages, without a useful link.
Places faith with mutual exhortation to patience and mercy, adding communal practice.
States human creation in pairs, without a relevant connection.
Shows obstinate refusal to believe despite signs, a repetitive negative contrast.
Connects faith with honest measures and social reform, an ethical consequence of belief.
Shows inherited power interests recast as reasons not to believe.
Immediate continuation: successful believers are humble and attentive in prayer.
Immediate continuation: they turn away from vain or futile speech and conduct.
Immediate continuation: they actively fulfill purification through almsgiving.
Immediate continuation: they guard their private parts.
Completes the lawful exception within the focus passage's ethic of chastity.
Marks transgression beyond those limits as the contrary to the successful believers' conduct.
Immediate continuation: they faithfully preserve trusts and covenants.
Immediate continuation: they carefully maintain their prayers.
Names the believers just described as the inheritors.
Completes the promised outcome: inheritance of al-Firdaws and abiding therein.
Explicitly calls those who obey God and the Messenger, fear God, and are mindful of Him successful.
Explicitly calls those who believe, honor, support, and follow the Messenger successful.
Completes 87:14 by joining remembrance of God and prayer to the successful person's purification.
Direct negative counterpart: one who corrupts the self has failed.
Directly announces a triumphant attainment for the God-conscious.
Defines the believers' lived practice through unseen faith, prayer, and spending.
Adds belief in revelation and the Hereafter to the profile whose conclusion is 2:5.
Completes 8:2 with prayer and spending as traits of true believers.
Promises believing righteous workers succession, security, and settled worship.
Distinguishes outward submission from faith that has truly entered hearts.
Defines the saving commitment as faith in God and His Messenger joined to striving.
States the forgiveness and gardens that result from that believing struggle as the great success.
Connects belief in God to expiation, gardens, and the declaration of supreme success.
Joins faith, righteous action, and belief in revelation with forgiveness and rectified condition.
Gives the final reward and divine pleasure for those who believe and do righteous deeds.
Gathers belief, worship, generosity, covenant-keeping, and patience into a comprehensive righteousness profile.
Makes a community that calls to good and restrains wrong the successful ones.
Commands piety and avoidance of usury so that people may succeed.
Calls the God-conscious toward forgiveness and a garden prepared for them.
Specifies generosity, restraint of anger, and pardon among the God-conscious qualities.
Links wrongdoing with remembrance, forgiveness, and refusal to persist.
Promises entry to Paradise to believers who do righteous deeds.
Promises forgiveness and great reward to those who believe and do righteous deeds.
Associates truthfulness with gardens, divine pleasure, and the great success.
Pairs faith and reform with freedom from fear and grief.
Connects piety and reform with freedom from fear and grief for Adam's descendants.
Elevates believers who migrate and strive for God above lesser claims.
Portrays believing men and women as mutual allies who establish worship and social good.
Shows believers giving their lives and wealth to God in the covenant that yields Paradise.
Says God guides believers who do righteous deeds by their faith.
Promises happiness and a good return to those who believe and do righteous deeds.
Promises a good life and better reward to every believing righteous worker.
Announces glad tidings of a great reward for believers who do righteous deeds.
Affirms that God does not waste the reward of believers who do good.
Exempts repentant believers who do righteous deeds and promises Paradise.
Describes the highest ranks for one who comes as a believer having done righteous deeds.
Assures that a believer's righteous work is not denied and is recorded.
Promises forgiveness and noble provision to believers who do righteous deeds.
Promises believers who do righteous deeds expiation and the best reward.
Promises gardens of refuge to believers who do righteous deeds.
Sets out a broad, paired profile of believing virtues and their promised forgiveness and reward.
Describes the chosen inheritors of the Book as including those foremost in good works.
Promises Paradise to every believer who does righteous work.
Promises angelic reassurance, Paradise, and steadfastness to those who affirm God and remain upright.
Describes the believers with the Messenger through worship, mercy, and a visible ethical mark.
Shows believing men and women receiving light and gardens on the Day of Judgment.
Calls those who believe in God and His messengers the truthful and witnessing ones.
Describes believers whose loyalty to God and His Messenger outranks hostile kinship, with promised success.
Calls believers to sincere repentance and promises expiation, gardens, and light.
Promises forgiveness and great reward to those who fear their Lord unseen.
Begins the exception to human anxiousness with those devoted to prayer.
Specifies constancy in prayer within that faithful exception.
Includes a known share in wealth for the needy among their qualities.
Completes the social recipients of that assigned share.
Reinforces trust and covenant-keeping, a direct match for 23:8.
Reinforces careful preservation of prayers, a direct match for 23:9.
Promises honored places in gardens to those displaying the preceding qualities.
Names fear of standing before the Lord and restraint from desire as the decisive ethical posture.
Gives Paradise as the refuge for the person described in 79:40.
